name: Asylum Under Article 26 of the 1962 Law on Foreigners

requirements.blocker_text: Article 26 of the 1962 Law on Foreigners allows asylum for anyone facing punishment for a political crime, or whose life or freedom is threatened, equally for political reasons. Article 27 gives an Asylum Committee, chaired by the Interior Minister, absolute discretion over the decision, with no right of appeal. In practice this law is almost never used -- asylum has reportedly been granted only once since enactment (a politicized 2000 case).

evidence_required.document: Evidence of political persecution or threat to life/freedom

outcome.duration_length: not specified in the source reviewed

sources.title: The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy (policy research institute) -- Lebanon's sole domestic asylum provision (Article 26/27 of the 1962 Law on Foreigners), Lebanon's non-ratification of the 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol, and the informal UNHCR-registration arrangement that functions as the de facto refugee system instead

THE MOST IMPORTANT DISCLOSURE FOR THIS COUNTRY, GIVEN LEBANON HOSTS ONE OF THE WORLD'S LARGEST REFUGEE POPULATIONS PER CAPITA: Lebanon has NOT ratified the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol. A domestic asylum provision does exist on paper (Article 26 of the 1962 Law on Foreigners) -- unlike India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka elsewhere in this dataset, which have no domestic asylum law at all -- but it is effectively dead letter: asylum has reportedly been granted only once since enactment, via an absolute-discretion, no-appeal Asylum Committee chaired by the Interior Minister. The real system operating on the ground is an informal one: a 2003 memorandum of understanding designates Lebanon a 'country of transit' rather than asylum, and UNHCR registers and cards refugees outside this domestic legal framework -- but the Lebanese government itself HALTED new UNHCR registrations in 2015, limiting recognized status to those who entered before cutoff dates (initially 1 January 2015, later extended to 24 April 2019), leaving only about 16% of refugees over 15 holding legal residency per the source reviewed. Syrian refugees (numbering well over a million) face this halted-registration regime plus periodic deportation pressure and discriminatory residency requirements; Palestinian refugees (present since 1948, numbering in the low hundreds of thousands) are governed by an entirely separate, decades-older set of arrangements tied to non-integration policy and Lebanon's internal power-sharing system, not detailed as its own route here since it is a distinct historical population rather than an ongoing 'route' a new applicant could pursue. This route is marked draft and should be read as describing a formally-existing-but-practically-inoperative legal category, not a realistic path to protection in Lebanon today. family_can_join set false (not asserted true without a source) since family-unity provisions specific to this Article 26 process were not detailed in the source reviewed.
